DC-2025-B260016.s: The law creates a program where certain groups, like businesses, nonprofits, and some event organizers, can ask for extra parking enforcement and pay the city back for it. It also lets campus police issue parking tickets in certain areas tied to their schools, if the school gives notice and the officer has training that matches the city’s rules. The District must also set rules for tracking tickets and handling how the money from these tickets is shared.

DC-2025-B260026.s: This bill would create a separate legal category for “theatrical wrestling” in the District. It defines theatrical wrestling as mock combat entertainment with a predetermined or choreographed outcome in a venue with fewer than 2,000 attendees, or at a festival or other special event. The bill would also exempt theatrical wrestling events from the Boxing and Wrestling Commission Act rules that apply to other events.

DC-2025-B260038.s: The bill would let the District’s Clemency Board waive the five-year waiting period for people seeking a pardon, but only if the federal Pardon Attorney or the President has already given that person a waiver. It would apply to pardon applicants who ask for the waiver, and the Board could still deny it. The Board could not grant a waiver to someone on probation, parole, or supervised release.

DC-2025-B260056.s: The bill would change how money from civil settlements for minor children is handled in the District of Columbia. It would require court approval for settlements worth $10,000 or more, and payment would go to a trustee and usually be placed in a blocked account until the child turns 18, with some court-approved options for other trusts or payment setups. A judge could still appoint a guardian of the child’s property if that is in the child’s best interest.

DC-2025-B260093.s: The measure would ban the sale or fee-based installation of solely battery-powered smoke detectors that are not tamper-resistant in the District starting July 1, 2025. It would also let people file a written complaint with the Mayor about a violation, even if an inspector did not see it happen. A violation could lead to a civil fine of up to $500, plus penalties and fees.

DC-2025-B260110.s: The bill would create a new Director of Recruitment and Retention in the Office of the City Administrator to find hard-to-fill jobs in District agencies and recommend ways to improve hiring and staff retention. It would let the Mayor offer up to $5,000 in recruitment incentives for new hires and retention payments for current workers in certain public safety and related jobs, and would require quarterly reports to the Council on hiring, departures, and money spent. It would also direct MPD, the Department of Corrections, and the Office of Unified Communications to run student outreach campaigns, and create an internship program at the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner for high school-age students.

DC-2025-B260167.s: The measure would stop health care entities in D.C. from charging fees for copies of personal medical records when they are needed for Social Security claims or appeals, or for other federal or District needs-based benefits or programs. It would apply when the records are requested by the patient, the patient’s representative, a nonprofit legal services worker, or the patient’s lawyer. It would take effect after mayoral approval, a 30-day congressional review period, and publication in the D.C. Register.

DC-2025-B260243.s: This act requires the Department of Energy and Environment to create a system to automatically enroll eligible households in its income-qualified utility affordability programs. It also requires the Department of Human Services and the Department of Health Care Finance to provide enrollment data for certain income-based programs, including TANF, SNAP, WIC, and Medicaid, so DOEE can use it for automatic enrollment. Households must give affirmative consent before being enrolled, may opt out at any time, and must be told they were enrolled, when benefits should start, and the expected monthly benefits.

DC-2025-B260325.s: This bill would amend D.C. ethics law to clarify the Board of Ethics and Government Accountability’s ability to require certain individuals to file public financial disclosures. It changes a definition that covers additional employees the Board may designate by rule, including people involved in contracting, procurement, grants or subsidies, policy, land use planning, inspections, licensing, regulation, or auditing. The bill would take effect only after mayoral approval or a Council override, plus congressional review.

DC-2025-B260361.s: The bill would phase out sales and distribution of mercury-containing compact fluorescent and linear fluorescent lamps in the District, with some narrow exceptions for things like medical, research, and special-use lamps. It would affect retailers and distributors, and the Department of Energy and the Environment would inspect stores, track complaints, and issue warnings or fines for violations. The limits would start on July 1, 2027 for some compact fluorescent lamps and on July 1, 2028 for other compact fluorescent lamps and linear fluorescent lamps.

DC-2025-B260420.s: The bill would require the Mayor to make sure local education agencies give student ID cards to every middle and high school student. The cards would show the school name, school year, student name, and a photo. It would apply to public school students in middle and high school.

DC-2025-B260427.s: The bill would require insurance licensees to keep a written cybersecurity program, do risk checks, and use safeguards to protect nonpublic information. It would also require prompt investigation of cybersecurity events and notice to the Department of Insurance, Securities, and Banking commissioner within 3 business days after one is found. The bill also makes a related change to the Freedom of Information Act.

DC-2025-B260428.s: The bill would update District rules on jobs for minors. It would ban work for children under 14, set hour limits for 14- to 17-year-olds, and require employers to post the rules and keep age and time records. It would give the Department of Employment Services the job of issuing youth work permits, checking workplaces, and enforcing the law, and it would let the Attorney General bring court cases over violations.

DC-2025-B260441.s: The bill would let the Mayor issue marriage licenses in D.C. during a total or partial federal government shutdown, when the Superior Court clerk is not issuing them. It would also let the Mayor authorize people who can perform weddings and keep the needed records until the court resumes that work. It mainly affects couples planning to marry and the officiants who handle the licenses.

DC-2025-B260444.s: The act changes the Food Policy Council’s report schedule from every year to every 3 years, starting September 30, 2027. It also gives the council more power to review food buying by District agencies and contractors that regularly buy food and drinks, and to set food purchasing standards and data-sharing rules. The changes apply to covered agencies and to the Office of Contracting and Procurement.

DC-2025-B260448.s: The bill would set rules for certain mortgage changes in the District of Columbia, including common changes like extending the loan term, lowering the interest rate, or reducing what is owed. It would say these covered changes do not change the mortgage’s priority and are not treated as a new loan. The rules would apply to both business and home mortgages.

DC-2025-B260495.s: The bill would change condo insurance rules for unit owners in the District of Columbia. It would require certain unit owner policies to include at least $25,000 in dwelling coverage, $500,000 in liability coverage, and $25,000 in loss assessment coverage, and it would raise the most a unit owner may owe for a condo insurance deductible to $25,000 when damage starts in that unit. It would also let a condo association charge a unit owner for that deductible amount, and if a unit owner does not keep the required insurance, the association could buy a policy and bill the owner for the premium.

DC-2025-B260524.s: The bill would add new criminal penalties for sharing false sexual images, videos, or audio made or changed with digital tools, including AI. It would apply to people in the District who knowingly share these images without consent, and it sets a felony for more serious cases and a misdemeanor for other cases. It also gives an exception for certain licensed communications companies and says the act would take effect after mayoral approval and a 60-day congressional review.

DC-2025-B260549.s: The bill would limit District help with federal immigration enforcement unless there is a judicial warrant or court order. It would bar District staff from giving transport to federal agents for immigration enforcement, doing civil immigration patrols or surveillance, and joining immigration enforcement at places like schools, hospitals, shelters, libraries, and some other service sites unless there are exigent circumstances. It would also require District employees to be trained on these rules.

DC-2025-B260589.s: This bill would symbolically designate the 4500 Block of Livingston Road, SE as William Brockenberry, Sr. Way. It would also symbolically designate the 4600 Block of Livingston Road, SE as William Brockenberry, Jr. Way.

DC-2025-B260597.s: The bill would create a new Housing Opportunity Fund for affordable housing in D.C. and split it into accounts for new building, subsidies, preservation, tenant purchases, and public land deals. It would also set rules for how the fund is used, reviewed, and audited, and create a board to help watch over it. The bill would let District retirement funds invest in local real estate, expand the District’s power to acquire land for housing, create a land purchase program and a revolving construction loan fund, and change some purchase rights for certain housing properties.

DC-2025-B260599.s: The bill would change the rules for the District’s emergency call center and fire and EMS medical director. It would spell out that the medical director oversees clinical parts of pre-hospital emergency medical services, including dispatch rules and quality checks. It would also require OUC call takers and dispatchers to get Emergency Medical Dispatch certification within one year of being hired, or within one year after the act takes effect for current staff.

DC-2025-B260602.s: The bill would change District rules for connecting solar systems to the electric grid. It would set clearer standards for costs, permitting times, and how electric companies handle solar interconnection requests for residents and other small solar projects. It would also create a help office at the Public Service Commission and let homeowners and renters plug in balcony solar systems without the same approval process as rooftop solar.

DC-2025-B260603.s: The bill would expand body camera release rules to cover cases where an MPD officer is present during a death or serious use of force by another law enforcement officer. It would also require MPD to include the names of other officers involved, when available, and to record details about other law enforcement officers at roll call. The department would have to share that roll call information with the Council committee chair on request, and some of it could be given to the public as summary data.

DC-2025-B260618.s: The bill would require D.C. police to record key details about every officer at an arrest scene, including names or badge numbers, whether any force was used, and how many officers did not identify themselves. It would also require the Mayor to release certain body camera video and a short incident description within 5 business days after a serious use of force by a federal officer, when D.C. police body cameras captured part of the event. The bill defines a federal law enforcement officer and would apply after approval, congressional review, and publication.

DC-2025-B260625.s: This bill would let the Mayor include proposed changes to the Future Land Use Map in a small area plan for the RFK Campus. It would also let those changes avoid some of the usual Comprehensive Plan review steps, but they would still have to be sent to the Council for consideration. It affects the RFK Campus and the planning process for that site.

DC-2025-B260642.s: This bill would close portions of the public alley system in Square 571 in Ward 6. The land would be treated as no longer needed for alley use, and title would vest as shown on the Surveyor’s plat. The alley closure would depend on all conditions in the official file for S.O. 25-01939 being met.

DC-2025-B260651.s: The bill would add the Downtown Arena and the Southeast Arena to District law that bans people from going onto a playing surface without permission. It would set plain names and addresses for those two arenas and apply the same no-entry rule to them. The rule would affect people at those arenas and the operators who can give permission.

DC-2025-B260697.s: This bill would change many reporting rules for the District Department of Energy and Environment and related laws. It would replace some report handoffs to the Council with posting the reports on agency websites, change deadlines, and make some reports less frequent or cover longer time spans. It would also end some outdated or repeated reporting rules.

DC-2025-B260705.s: This bill would symbolically designate 48th Place, N.W., between MacArthur Blvd, N.W. and V St., N.W., in Ward 3, as "William "Spence" Spencer, IV Way." It is meant to honor William Hall Spencer, IV for his work in the Palisades community and his service in other places. The designation would affect that street area in the District of Columbia.

DC-2025-B260725.s: The measure would make the District of Columbia Department of Health set up a digital system for schools and health care providers to send student health and dental health forms. It would also stop providers from charging parents or guardians for those certificates. The bill would create a tiered fee plan for health professional licenses and registrations based on how much schooling the job needs.

DC-2025-B260733.s: Enacted in the District of Columbia, this temporary act changes the deadline for the Prearrest Diversion Task Force to give its first recommendations on prearrest diversion for certain misdemeanor offenses and groups of people. It sets one deadline at no later than June 2025 and another at no later than July 31, 2026. The act takes effect after mayoral approval and congressional review, and it expires after 225 days.

DC-2025-B260735.s: The law requires the District Department of Corrections to provide a free public education for certain people in its custody who have disabilities and are held in secure facilities. It applies to people age 18 through the end of their school eligibility under federal disability law and District law. The rule covers school years 2025-2026 and 2026-2027, and the act was signed and enacted on October 21, 2026.

DC-2025-B260783.s: The measure would treat broadband providers as meeting District price disclosure rules if they already follow certain federal broadband label rules from Jan. 1, 2026. It would apply starting Sept. 26, 2026, and it would expire after 225 days. It affects broadband internet providers in the District.

DC-2025-B260784.s: The act became law and makes short-term changes to police complaint rules and some District criminal law terms. It would expand the Police Complaints Board to 9 members and let the Office of Police Complaints’ Executive Director start a complaint based on evidence they find, including missed reports or failure to step in when another officer used excessive force or broke rules. It also changes some District law language so certain provisions apply only to victims under 18.

DC-2025-B260790.s: The measure would direct the Department of Small and Local Business Development to give a $1 million grant in Fiscal Year 2027 to the Duke Business Improvement District Corporation. The money would support work in the Greater Shaw/U Street area for property owners, businesses, residents, and visitors. It is a temporary law and would expire after 225 days.

DC-2025-B260798.s: The bill would change District rules for MOST forms, which are medical forms that record a patient’s treatment wishes. It would let more health workers help prepare and sign these forms, including advanced practice nurses, naturopathic physicians, and physician assistants under delegation agreements, and it would update the MOST Advisory Committee. It would also require completed MOST forms to be put in the patient’s electronic medical record and kept as part of the permanent record until revoked.

DC-2025-B260799.s: The measure would update District rules for health care facilities and providers, including assisted living residences, home care agencies, and other licensed health care entities. It would require reporting of adverse events and cybersecurity events, add patient safety group participation, and let the health department use stronger fines and inspections in some cases. It would also add some new licensing rules, clarify ownership disclosure, and allow some fee changes tied to inflation.

DC-2025-B260806.s: The bill would symbolically rename the 600 Block of Alabama Avenue, S.E., as Mary Cuthbert Way. It affects that block in the District of Columbia. It would take effect after mayoral approval and a 30-day congressional review period.

DC-2025-B260807.s: The bill would symbolically name the unit block of Atlantic Street, S.E., as Constance “Connie” Mobley Way. It affects that street block in the District of Columbia. The change would take effect after mayoral approval and a 30-day congressional review period.

DC-2025-B260809.s: This bill would make technical and clarifying changes to the Health Benefit Exchange Authority’s law. It would update the Authority’s purposes, board membership, staff compensation rules, and ethics and conflict-of-interest rules. It would also add one board member with expertise in information technology, including artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and system architecture.

DC-2025-B260810.s: This bill would symbolically rename C Street, NE, between 4th Street, NE, and 6th Street, NE, as "Veola Jackson Way." It affects that stretch of street in the District of Columbia and would take effect only after mayoral approval, a possible veto override, a 30-day congressional review, and publication in the District register.

DC-2025-B260811.s: The bill would open and name several new streets in Square 1112-E in Ward 7, including 20th Street, 21st Street, Burke Street, 20th Place, 21st Place, C Place, and C Street. It would also close a small part of 20th Street, S.E. These changes are meant to support construction in the Hill East area, and the fiscal note says funds are available, with future road upkeep expected to cost about $1 million every five years.

DC-2025-B260812.s: The measure would remove part of the highway plan from land at 601 Mississippi Ave. SE in Square 5963, Lots 801, 802, and 803, and add part of Valley Avenue, SE, to the plan on Lot 801. It is tied to the renovation of Hart Middle School by the Department of General Services. If approved, it would take effect after mayoral approval, a 30-day congressional review, and publication in the District of Columbia Register.

DC-2025-B260814.s: The measure would symbolically name the 700-800 block of Euclid Street NW, between Sherman Avenue NW and Georgia Avenue NW in Ward 1, as Dolores Tucker Way. It would honor Dolores Tucker by giving that street block her name. The act would take effect after mayoral approval, council override if needed, a 30-day congressional review, and publication in the District of Columbia Register.

DC-2025-B260816.s: The bill would make technical updates to the rules for the D.C. Public Library and its Board of Library Trustees. It would update old job titles, let the board elect its chair every two years, and treat the library’s answers to Council oversight questions as its annual report. It would also spell out how the board can handle permits, fees, and fee waivers for private revenue-making use of library property.

DC-2025-B260817.s: The bill would symbolically rename the public alley system in Square 1030 next to Lots 812 and 814 as “Electric Way.” It affects that alley area in Ward 6. The act would take effect after mayoral approval, a 30-day congressional review period, and publication in the District of Columbia Register.

DC-2025-B260819.s: The measure would require some condo associations to get reserve studies on repair and replacement costs and to update them every 5 years. It would also change how some inclusionary housing units are sold by giving the seller an equity payment on later resales, and it would change home purchase aid so lenders help with qualification while the Mayor makes the final call. It would create a local mortgage foreclosure prevention program and fund it with fees on home closings and foreclosure filings.

DC-2025-B260820.s: The bill would require the Mayor to send the Office of Tax and Revenue a list of District properties with affordability rules, including affordable housing and inclusionary zoning. It is meant to help property tax assessments reflect the lower rent limits on those homes. It affects owners of affordable housing and other properties with District-imposed affordability limits.

DC-2025-B260822.s: The bill would require the Mayor to hire an outside reviewer to study the District’s housing development costs and rules. The study would compare DC with nearby counties in Maryland and Virginia and measure things like total cost per unit, permit time, fees, taxes during construction, and other major delays. It would also point to rules that add cost or delay, say whether they are unique to DC or higher here than elsewhere, and recommend changes. The Mayor would then send the study to the Council within 30 days after it is finished.

DC-2025-B260826.s: The bill would change the rules for school breakfast in the District on a temporary basis. It would let schools use grab-and-go breakfast, breakfast served in the classroom, or both. The change would apply to District school breakfast service and would last for 225 days after it takes effect.

DC-2025-B260827.s: The act would let District residents apply for a block party permit to close a street for a Porchfest, which is a neighborhood music festival on private property or nearby public space with no fee. It also adds Porchfest to the District’s block party rules and says the District should approve block parties, including Porchfests. The emergency act became law and lasts for no more than 90 days.

DC-2025-B260829.s: This bill would create a pilot program for certain eviction cases based on nonpayment of rent in the District. It would require early mediation between landlords and tenants, and housing providers in the program would have to send a Notice of Diversion Rights in eligible cases before filing to evict. The bill would also create a fund for District assistance tied to mediation agreements, including rental assistance or moving expenses in some cases. It would let the Department award grants for housing counseling services or same-day legal representation for tenants in the program.

DC-2025-B260834.s: This bill would declare two District-owned properties at 2000 14th Street NW and 1414 V Street NW surplus and authorize the Mayor to dispose of them. It would allow a selected developer to build a mixed-use project that includes a new NAACP headquarters, housing, a hotel, and other uses. The bill also requires some residential units to be affordable, and it would require agreements for Certified Business Enterprises and a First Source Agreement.

DC-2025-B260838.s: The bill would symbolically name the 1500 block of 45th Street NE, between Douglass Street NE and Quarles Street NE in Ward 7, as "Kentrell Devaughn Way." It would honor Kentrell Devaughn, a Ward 7 resident, on the street where he was born and raised. The act would take effect after mayoral approval or a Council veto override, plus a 30-day congressional review period.

DC-2025-B260839.s: The bill would symbolically name 50th Street NE, between East Capitol Street NE and Ames Street NE in Ward 7, as "Johnny Gant Way." It is meant to honor Johnny Gant, a longtime Ward 7 resident, boxer, businessman, coach, and mentor. The change would take effect after mayoral approval and a 30-day congressional review period.

DC-2025-B260840.s: The Council would approve an emergency, multiyear reimbursable agreement with the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority to design and build station improvements at the Stadium-Armory Metrorail Station. The agreement would cover fiscal years 2026 through 2030 and total $300 million. The act would take effect after mayoral approval or a council override and last for up to 90 days.

DC-2025-B260843.s: The bill would change how Events DC’s excess cash is figured out under District law. It would exclude certain funds from that calculation and update how debt service and operating costs are counted. The changes would affect Events DC and the money it transfers to the District’s General Fund.

DC-2025-B260844.s: The bill would let the District issue bonds to pay for renovation costs at Nationals Park. The total amount would not be more than $410 million, and up to $380 million of that would go to the project costs. It would affect the District, the stadium renovation project, and the fund used to help pay the bonds.

DC-2025-B260845.s: The bill would let the Mayor give up two land parcels at Poplar Point and buy Lot 1041 in Square 5860. It is tied to a land swap that would help move National Park Service facilities and add a new entry point by extending Howard Road. The Mayor’s power to dispose of the two parcels would end 10 years after the act takes effect.

DC-2025-B260847.s: This emergency measure would change the District’s green building rules for some District-owned and District-funded projects. It would exempt certain projects from net-zero-energy rules, update which projects must meet them, and set new rules for some new buildings and major alterations called Level 3 alterations, which are bigger building changes. It also would change deadlines for final rules on net-zero energy and on-site fuel use, which means burning fuel at the building for heat.

DC-2025-B260848.s: The measure would make an emergency change to D.C. rules for for-hire vehicles and clarify who counts as a private vehicle-for-hire operator. It says this is a person who uses a company’s digital dispatch system to drive a motor vehicle and give rides to passengers. The change would apply as of March 1, 2024.

DC-2025-B260849.s: The measure would let the Mayor write rules to carry out the Language Access Act of 2004. It applies on an emergency basis because of congressional review and would take effect after mayoral approval, or after a council override of a veto. The act would be in force for no more than 90 days.

DC-2025-B260852.s: The bill would approve an emergency contract between the University of the District of Columbia and Ellucian Company LLC. The contract is for $10,157,746 and would help move the university’s enterprise resource planning system to a software-as-a-service setup, which means a web-based service. It would apply to the university.

DC-2025-B260854.s: The bill would make Saint Elizabeths Hospital an independent District agency run by a 13-member board. It would also create a patient safety and rights committee, add more patient rights and reporting rules, and set up a separate hospital fund. The change would move hospital control from the Department of Behavioral Health, with the transfer planned for October 1, 2028, or later if the Council sets a later date.

DC-2025-B260855.s: The measure would let the District create and run the Duke Business Improvement District, a local area where property owners pay extra fees for shared services. It sets the district’s boundary and lists the property types and tax rates that would apply, including rates for hotels, housing units, parking lots, and religious buildings. It also sets board membership rules and allows matching funds from the Greater U Street Parking Benefit Fund.

DC-2025-B260856.s: Student ID cards issued by local education agencies for middle and high school students would also work as District of Columbia Public Library cards. They would also allow entry to Department of Parks and Recreation facilities and list how to contact the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. The cards would be free.

DC-2025-B260857.s: The Council would approve an emergency grant deal with the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority. It would let the District provide capital funding for rail and bus repair needs from Oct. 1, 2026, through Sept. 30, 2032. The funding would be up to $178.5 million each year, for a total of up to $1.071 billion.

DC-2025-B260861.s: The bill would let the Mayor extend two District property leases. One is for Dupont Underground, extending the lease from November 18, 2029, to November 18, 2042. The other is for the Anacostia Boathouse site at 1900 M Street, S.E., extending the lease from June 7, 2030, to June 7, 2047.

DC-2025-B260863.s: This emergency bill would update District rules so a transition committee can be set up for the Mayor-elect and use the same meaning of "Mayor-elect" in related rules. It defines "Mayor-elect" as the person certified as the winner of the 2026 mayoral election, or before that the unofficial winner if the margin is at least 2%. If approved, it would take effect right away and stay in place for up to 90 days.

DC-2025-B260874.s: The bill would rename a part of the public alley in Square 1063, next to Lots 85, 86, and 817, as Matthews Court. It would affect that alley area in the District of Columbia and is meant to honor the Matthews family.

DC-2025-B260875.s: The measure would change how District parking and traffic tickets are handled, including tickets from automated traffic cameras and some parking, standing, stopping, and pedestrian offenses. It would remove one added penalty for not answering some notices within 30 days, and it would set a 60-day answer period for notices of infraction in another part of the law. People with these tickets, and some vehicle lessors, would be affected.

DC-2025-B260877.s: The measure would require the District’s corrections department to restore regular in-person contact visits at the Correctional Treatment Facility within 120 days and start a phased pilot for contact visits at the Central Detention Facility within 240 days. It would also set rules for when visits can be limited, require clear scheduling and visitor-approval steps, and call for family and disability accommodations. The bill would affect people held at those two facilities, their approved visitors, and the corrections department.

DC-2025-B260878.s: This bill would approve two amendments to the Hospital Operations Agreement for Cedar Hill Regional Medical Center. The amendments would set a process for subsidy payments based on the hospital’s operating deficit in its first year and would provide support for maternal and fetal care services. It would affect the District government and UHS East End Sub, LLC, the hospital’s operating entity.

DC-2025-B260881.s: This bill would change how certain grant money can be used, so it could be used to buy real property or make capital improvements to real property. It would also let DFHV write rules to carry out a carrier-for-hire support surcharge. The changes would apply to the District’s grant-making and taxicab-related rules.

DC-2025-B260882.s: This bill would change how certain grant funds can be used, allowing them for the purchase of or capital improvements to real property. It would also allow DFHV to issue rules to carry out a carrier-for-hire support surcharge. The changes would affect grant funding and taxicab and carrier-for-hire regulation in the District of Columbia.

DC-2025-CER260231.s: The resolution would recognize and honor Amber Gove for her years of service to Advisory Neighborhood Commission 6A, Ward 6, and the District of Columbia. It says she led neighborhood work on community issues, street safety, school input, and local meetings. The resolution would take effect immediately.

DC-2025-CER260232.s: The Council of the District of Columbia would recognize and celebrate Old City Market and Oven for its 10th anniversary. It would honor the business for its food, drinks, welcoming space, and support for neighbors and the Capitol Hill community. The resolution would take effect right away.

DC-2025-CER260233.s: This resolution recognizes and acknowledges Ann Chisholm’s professional contributions as she retires from the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority. It says she worked there for more than 20 years and served in community relations and government relations roles. It also notes her work connecting WMATA with District government and outreach to Advisory Neighborhood Commissioners.

DC-2025-CER260234.s: This resolution recognizes and congratulates Saint Martin of Tours Catholic Church on its 125th anniversary. It honors the church’s long record of faith, education, fellowship, and service to District residents. The resolution also notes the church’s work in worship, schools, community outreach, charitable ministries, and partnerships that have helped people of different ages and backgrounds.

DC-2025-CER260235.s: The resolution would declare November 20, 2026, as Transgender Day of Remembrance in the District of Columbia. It would recognize transgender people, honor those lost to violence, and note the community’s resilience. The resolution would take effect when it is first published in the District of Columbia Register.

DC-2025-CER260236.s: This resolution would honor and celebrate the life and service of Talib Shakir, a District resident who helped returning citizens rebuild their lives after incarceration. It recognizes his work in city government, including roles in community relations, safer neighborhoods, and the Office on Returning Citizen Affairs. The Council also expresses condolences to his family and others who loved him.

DC-2025-CER260237.s: This resolution celebrates Dr. Lonnie G. Bunch III for his work as the 14th Secretary of the Smithsonian Institution and for his contributions to the Smithsonian and the nation. It also declares November 18 as "Dr. Lonnie Bunch III Day."

DC-2025-CER260238.s: This resolution recognizes Shanel Wilson for her service as Deputy Chief of Staff to Councilmember Robert C. White, Jr. It says she helped with staff management, communications, constituent services, and community events. It also says she helped respond to residents’ concerns and requests for assistance.

DC-2025-CER260239.s: This ceremonial resolution recognizes Jasmine Joyner for her work as Senior Executive Assistant and Constituent Services Coordinator in Councilmember Robert C. White, Jr.’s office. It says she helped residents get guidance, answers from District agencies, and help with housing and building-condition concerns. The resolution also says she helped with meetings, events, and daily office operations.

DC-2025-CER260240.s: This resolution recognizes Whitney Sweetwine for her service as Communications Director to Councilmember Robert C. White, Jr. It says her work helped the office communicate with residents, explain policy issues, and keep the public informed. It also honors her role in supporting transparent, accessible, and effective District government.

DC-2025-CER260241.s: This resolution recognizes Jaya Pillai for her leadership as Legislative and Committee Director in the office of Councilmember Robert C. White, Jr. It says she helped with the Council’s legislative and oversight work, including hearings, oversight, budget review, stakeholder engagement, and work on housing programs and policies.

DC-2025-CER260242.s: This resolution recognizes Jakaila Davis for her service as Legislative Clerk in Councilmember Robert C. White, Jr.’s office. It says she helps with legislative work, education matters, and issues about pets in housing. The resolution also recognizes her behind-the-scenes coordination and her contributions to policy work and office operations.

DC-2025-CER260243.s: This ceremonial resolution recognizes Prita Piekara for her leadership as Chief of Staff to Councilmember Robert C. White, Jr. It says she helped lead the office’s work on legislation, oversight, constituent service, and communication with residents across the District of Columbia.

DC-2025-CER260244.s: This resolution recognizes Maurice Cates II for his service as a Legislative Assistant to Councilmember Robert C. White, Jr. It also recognizes his work on building conditions, housing, executive administration and labor, public works and operations, and public safety work. The Council says he has helped with legislative research, policy development, oversight preparation, and coordination across these areas.

DC-2025-CER260245.s: This resolution recognizes Francesca Bryce for her service as Senior Legislative Counsel to Councilmember Robert C. White, Jr. It says she has worked on housing, justice and public safety, returning citizens, and youth affairs. It also honors her work across Council committees and her service to District residents.

DC-2025-CER260246.s: This resolution recognizes Christian Wiskur for his service as Deputy Legislative and Committee Director to Councilmember Robert C. White, Jr. It says he has led work on housing finance, community development, economic development, tax policy, and matters concerning the RFK campus. The resolution also notes his role in helping with legislative strategy, hearings, budget decisions, and Council deliberations.

DC-2025-CER260247.s: This resolution recognizes Kate Conquest for her service as Senior Legislative Assistant to Councilmember Robert C. White, Jr. It says she led work on housing authority oversight and tenant advocacy, and also handled health, transportation, and environmental policy. The resolution says her work supported District residents.

DC-2025-CER260248.s: This resolution recognizes Sean Cuddihy for his service to the Council of the District of Columbia and his work on housing, budgeting, and oversight. It says he helped with the Committee on Housing, the Committee on Government Operations and Facilities, and later the Committee on Public Works and Operations. It also recognizes his work on public accountability and his continued service to District residents.

DC-2025-CER260250.s: This resolution recognizes, remembers, and celebrates the life of Antonio “Tony” Campanaro, the owner of Tony’s Barber Shop. It says he was a local barber for 55 years in the Tenleytown and Van Ness neighborhoods and served generations of families. The resolution also says he was important to those communities.

DC-2025-CER260253.s: This resolution recognizes, honors, and celebrates Lorenzo Clifton Brown on the occasion of his 100th birthday. It says he served in the United States Navy, has lived in the District since the 1950s, worked in construction, and continued masonry and community garden work after retiring.

DC-2025-CER260254.s: This resolution recognizes the Department of Aging and Community Living for supporting older adults in the District of Columbia. It mentions services and programs such as community activities, nutrition and transportation services, healthcare and insurance counseling, caregiver support, adult protective services, senior wellness centers, and help for seniors with memory-related illnesses.

DC-2025-CER260255.s: The Council recognizes the District of Columbia Department of Human Resources for its work in strengthening the District government’s workforce and advancing employee development. It says the department supports recruitment, retention, professional growth, and human resource management for District public servants and agencies. The resolution also notes the department’s role in benefits, retirement, staffing, and other personnel services.

DC-2025-CER260257.s: This resolution recognizes the Office of the Inspector General for its oversight of District agencies and its work on accounting, auditing, financial oversight, investigations, inspections, and recommendations. It says the office helps promote accountability, integrity, transparency, and public confidence in the DC government. The resolution also thanks the leadership and staff for their independent oversight and responsible stewardship of public funds.

DC-2025-CER260260.s: This resolution honors the Office of Employee Appeals for giving impartial, legally sufficient, and timely decisions on appeals filed by District of Columbia government employees. It says the office provides independent review of personnel actions and helps support fairness, accountability, and due process in District government. The Council also extends gratitude to the office’s leadership and staff for their service and commitment to public service.

DC-2025-PR260544.s: This resolution would approve transferring jurisdiction over about 709 square feet of land from the United States Department of the Interior, National Park Service, to the District of Columbia. The land is part of Reservation 357 and Lot 1008 in Square 1299. The transfer is to support redevelopment of a vacant office building into a mainly multifamily residential building and to allow access to the building.

DC-2025-PR260717.s: The resolution confirms Niranjan Adhikari as a member of the District of Columbia Commission on Human Rights. His term would run until December 31, 2027, and the resolution took effect right away.

DC-2025-PR260718.s: The resolution confirms Monika Nemeth as a member of the District of Columbia Commission on Human Rights. Her term would end on December 31, 2028. It takes effect right away.

DC-2025-PR260743.s: The resolution would confirm Mikyala Moore as the Ward 8 member of the Police Complaints Board. She would fill a vacant seat for the rest of the term, which ends January 12, 2029.

DC-2025-PR260809.s: The resolution approved Contract No. CW130810 with Capitol Paving of D.C., Inc. and authorized payment for snow and ice removal services. It says the contract was increased to a total estimated amount of $5 million, and that Council approval was needed because the value was over $1 million in a 12-month period. The resolution took effect immediately.

DC-2025-PR260810.s: This resolution would approve the Robert F. Kennedy Campus Master Plan as a small area action plan. The plan would guide development of the RFK campus area and provide supplemental guidance to the Zoning Commission and other District agencies. It covers land along the Anacostia River and includes housing, streets, parks, open spaces, and transportation connections.

DC-2025-PR260826.s: The Council declared an emergency to quickly update rules for the mayoral transition. It would add a clear definition of "Mayor-elect" to ethics and official mail rules, and it would say a transition committee may be organized for the Mayor-elect. The resolution took effect right away.

DC-2025-PR260828.s: The Council would declare an emergency so it can quickly change the date for the Prearrest Diversion Task Force to issue its first recommendations. The change would affect how the task force handles prearrest diversion for certain misdemeanor offenses and groups of people in the District. The resolution says this is needed to avoid a gap in the law while federal review is pending.

DC-2025-PR260830.s: This resolution says there is an emergency need to approve a multiyear contract with Reworld Fairfax, LLC. The contract would let the District get municipal solid waste disposal services through the Office of Contracting and Procurement for the Department of Public Works. It says the 4-year base term would cost $46,818,000.

DC-2025-PR260831.s: This resolution would approve an emergency multiyear contract with Reworld Fairfax, LLC. The contract is for municipal solid waste disposal services and is for $46,818,000 for the 4-year base term. It affects the District’s waste disposal services and the Council’s approval of the contract.

DC-2025-PR260832.s: This resolution would approve two amendments to the hospital operations agreement for Cedar Hill Regional Medical Center. It would set a process for a support payment from the Hospital Fund if the hospital operated at a deficit in its first year, and it would provide support for maternal and fetal care services. The changes affect the District and UHS East End Sub, LLC, the hospital operator.

DC-2025-PR260833.s: This proposed resolution would let the District issue, sell, and deliver tax-exempt revenue bonds, notes, or other obligations of up to $47.075 million. The money would help Volunteers of America Chesapeake & Carolinas, Inc. finance, refinance, or reimburse costs for acquiring, rehabilitating, and building facilities in the District, Maryland, and Virginia. The bonds would not be general obligations of the District and would not involve the District’s full faith and credit or taxing power.

DC-2025-PR260834.s: This resolution declares an emergency to allow the District to authorize tax-exempt revenue bonds, notes, or other obligations up to $275 million. The money would help Madrone finance the conversion of a vacant office building at 600 E Street, NW into about 415 apartments for college students, faculty, and staff. The project would also include ground floor retail, equipment and furnishings, and underground parking spaces.

DC-2025-PR260835.s: This resolution would authorize the District to issue up to $275 million in revenue bonds and loan the proceeds to Madrone – DC Student Housing I, LLC. The money would help finance a project that converts a vacant office building at 600 E Street, NW into 415 apartments for college students, faculty, and staff. The project also includes ground floor retail, underground parking, and other related costs.

DC-2025-PR260836.s: This resolution says there is an emergency need to approve the issuance of bonds and notes for the New Communities Initiative. The bonds and notes would help finance, refinance, make loans for, or reimburse costs of New Communities Initiative projects. The initiative covers Barry Farm, Lincoln Heights-Richardson Dwellings, Northwest One, and Park Morton, including the Bruce Monroe redevelopment.

DC-2025-PR260837.s: This resolution would approve the emergency issuance and sale of income tax secured bonds or notes to support New Communities Initiative projects. The money would help finance, refinance, make loans for, or reimburse costs for the redevelopment plans for Northwest One, Lincoln Heights/Richardson Dwellings, Barry Farm/Park Chester/Wade Road, and Park Morton. The total principal amount could not exceed $318,826,350.

DC-2025-PR260839.s: This resolution declares an emergency so the Council can act quickly on changes tied to the Fiscal Year 2027 Budget Support Act. It would expand how a grant to the Rosemount Center may be used, including for capital improvements. It would also allow rulemaking to carry out a surcharge on certain carrier-for-hire trips.
